# 1. KV Cache: The Foundation of Generative Inference

### Concept & Mechanics
Autoregressive language models generate text token-by-token. Computing the probability distribution over the next token given the entire preceding context $(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_t)$ conventionally requires recomputing all intermediate representations from scratch at every step.

### Concept & Mechanics
Autoregressive language models generate text token-by-token. Computing the probability distribution over the next token given the entire preceding context $(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_t)$ conventionally requires recomputing all past layer activations. Because hidden states at layer $l$ depend on all prior tokens, recomputation is $O(t)$ per generated token, leading to $O(t^2)$ total compute.

# 1. KV Caches: The Core Memory Engine

### Mechanism
During autoregressive generation, LLMs predict the next token by conditioning on all previously generated tokens. Mathematically, the forward pass computes Key ($K$) and Value ($V$) tensors for each token. Storing these per-token representations in memory is the **Key-Value (KV) Cache**.

When generating token $t$:
1. The model takes the input token embedding, passes it through the layers, and generates $K_t, V_t$.
2. To compute the attention score for token $t$, the Query ($Q_t$) is dotted with *all* previous keys $K_0, K_1, \dots, K_{t-1}$, yielding an attention map.
3. The attention map is multiplied by all previous values $V_0, V_1, \dots, V_{t-1}$ to produce the context vector.
